archetype.name: Game Manager (spot starter)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup running a run-first, defense-led offense on low volume who keeps the ball out of harm's way, feeds his top receiver and has hit a handful of deep shots that inflate his efficiency.

report.headline: Career-best efficiency on a small, soft sample; San Francisco is the real test.
report.take:
Drew Lock is an eighth-year backup, and his career has been consistent: below-average accuracy and middling-to-poor efficiency wherever he went. His completion percentage over expected was negative in every season in the dossier, bottoming out at -6.1 with the Giants in 2024, when he also posted -0.136 EPA per play. In 2020, his one long run as a starter, he threw 15 interceptions, 58th of 59. This season he has been the opposite: 0.303 EPA per dropback (3rd of 55), a +6.24 CPOE, 9.0 yards per attempt and no interceptions on 93 throws, mostly in games he started or finished in relief for Sam Darnold.

Three things drive it. The first is Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who has drawn 41 of his targets at 0.702 EPA each, the bulk of everything Lock has produced. The second is a few deep balls: nine throws of 20+ air yards produced 18.4 EPA, more than half of his dropback total, with three touchdowns. The third is the setting. Seattle runs more than situations call for (-5.2 pass rate over expected, 28th), its defense ranks 6th in EPA, and Lock's four games came against Arizona twice (31st in defensive EPA today), Las Vegas (28th) and New England (24th). Every one of those games went under the total. He has thrown about two dozen times a game, mostly in one-score or comfortable situations, against defenses that rarely punished anything.

The numbers hide how little of this has been tested. The tracking profile is conservative: 7.56 intended air yards and a target depth just short of the sticks. His underneath game (0.237 EPA on throws under 10 air yards) is solid, but it is the deep column that turns good into top-three. The red zone has been below average per play (-0.055) despite three touchdowns. The Raiders game was the warning sign. He was pressured on 36.4% of dropbacks, took three sacks and lost two fumbles, on a day right tackle Abraham Lucas was knocked out. Left tackle Charles Cross and guard Quenton Nelson are now listed out as well.

Going forward, his value depends on one thing: Darnold's quadriceps. Darnold is listed out but suited up for Monday's unofficial practice, with an expected return date of the 49ers game itself. If Darnold plays, Lock goes back to the bench. If Lock starts at San Francisco, he faces the best offense in the league as a road underdog, behind a line that may be missing its left side. Expect the efficiency to come back toward average even if the poise holds.

strengths.title: Clean, accurate decision-making
strengths.body: He has not thrown an interception on 93 attempts, and his bad-throw rate ranks 7th of 45 charted passers. Both are sharp breaks from a career of negative CPOE. Some of that comes from a quick, short-leaning approach in a scheme that keeps him on schedule. The zero-interception mark will not hold over a real sample, but the low-risk approach is a choice he can keep making.

strengths.title: Smith-Njigba as the engine
strengths.body: His top receiver has drawn 41 targets at 0.702 EPA each, and throws over the middle have produced 0.698 EPA per attempt with five touchdowns. That connection is the most repeatable part of his production. It depends on the receiver's skill and the scheme, not on Lock reinventing himself. As long as Smith-Njigba is on the field, Lock has a dependable first read.

strengths.title: Third downs at distance
strengths.body: He has converted half his third downs with an average of 7.4 yards to go, at 0.513 EPA per play with four touchdowns. Converting at that distance means he has been willing to throw past the sticks when it counts, even though his overall target depth sits short of them. On 32 plays it is a hint rather than a law, but it is the best sign that his production is more than dink-and-dunk.

concerns.title: Deep-ball spike on nine throws
concerns.body: Nine attempts of 20+ air yards account for 18.4 EPA, more than half of his dropback total, with a +27.3 CPOE on them. Nothing in his career suggests he is this accurate downfield; his 2024 CPOE was -6.1. This is the part of his line most likely to regress, and when it does his overall efficiency falls from top-three to merely good.

concerns.title: Built against bottom-tier defenses
concerns.body: Two of his four games came against Arizona, 31st in defensive EPA, plus Las Vegas at 28th and New England at 24th. He has not faced a competent defense or played from behind for long; trailing by nine or more he has seven snaps. The production is real, but it was earned in the friendliest conditions possible.

concerns.title: Pressure and the ball behind a depleted line
concerns.body: Seattle's quarterbacks get hit more than almost anyone's (29th in hit rate allowed). In the Raiders game Lock was pressured on 36.4% of dropbacks and lost two fumbles. With Cross and Nelson listed out and Lucas questionable, that is the likely environment for any start. Ball security under pressure is a real flaw to watch, not just bad luck.

trend.note: He posted positive passing EPA in every game, peaking against Arizona in Week 2. His last three games ran slightly above his season rates (+0.042 EPA per dropback). The bigger swings have been in his role, in and out of the lineup around Darnold, not in his play.

nextGame.headline: Road underdog against the league's best offense, line in pieces
nextGame.body:
San Francisco's defense is 10th in EPA and much tougher on the ground (5th against the run, 1st in explosive runs allowed). Seattle's run game is already 30th, so this likely lands on Lock's arm with long-yardage downs. The pass defense is middling (16th), with a soft spot underneath (20th in short-throw EPA) and a stingier deep game (5th). That pushes him toward his quick game and away from the deep shots that inflated his numbers. It is the league's lowest sack-rate defense, a real break for a patched line. Smith-Njigba's role is the open one: opposing WR1s have done slightly better than usual here, while WR2s have been held furthest under their averages in the league. Running backs see more of the targets against this defense than usual.

Availability decides everything. Darnold is listed out but practiced Monday with a return date of game day; if he is cleared, Lock does not start. Lock is questionable himself. Cross and Nelson are out and Lucas is questionable, which could leave three line starters missing. On the other side, linebacker Dre Greenlaw is out, Nate Hobbs is on IR and corner Deommodore Lenoir is questionable with a foot injury. That thins the coverage Lock would face. The 49ers' offense, the best in the league by EPA and pass EPA, is missing right tackle Colton McKivitz, but the Book still has them favored by 3 with a 46.5 total. That points to Seattle having to throw more than it wants.

keyMatchups.title: Quiet rush vs patched protection
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco generates the fewest sacks in the league, which eases the worry of a Seattle line that allows hits at the 29th-ranked rate. If the interior holds without Nelson, Lock gets a clean enough pocket to work. If the edges break down the way they did in Las Vegas, the fumbles come back.

keyMatchups.title: Underneath space, deep lid
keyMatchups.body: The 49ers give up more on short throws (20th) than deep ones (5th). That matches the steadier half of Lock's game, his under-10 throws at 0.237 EPA. Expect fewer of the deep shots that made his season and more short completions to Smith-Njigba and the backs.

keyMatchups.title: Game script against the top offense
keyMatchups.body: Seattle normally hides its passer behind a run-heavy plan, but its run game meets a top-five run defense while San Francisco's offense leads the league in pass EPA. Falling behind would push Lock into the trailing, obvious-passing downs he has barely seen. That raises his volume and his risk together.

nextGame.watch: Whether Darnold is cleared. If Lock starts, watch whether Seattle can keep him out of long-yardage, trailing downs early.

restOfSeason.body:
His outlook depends on Darnold's health more than on anything he does. With Darnold already practicing and an expected return date at the 49ers game, the most likely path is Lock back at QB2, called on for spot starts or relief. When he does play, expect the parts that held up across all four games to carry over: quick decisions, the Smith-Njigba connection and low turnover-worthy throwing. The deep-ball surge, the zero interceptions and a top-three EPA rank are not sustainable. They were built on nine deep throws and the league's softest defenses, and they run against a career of negative CPOE.

If he starts, a fair expectation is roughly 175 to 235 passing yards a game on 24 to 32 attempts, with one to two touchdowns more often than not. His efficiency should settle toward slightly-above-average rather than elite, and turnovers are more likely behind a thinned line.

confidence.note: 93 attempts against bottom-tier defenses, an outlier against his career, and a role that hinges on Darnold's quad.
